newsitem.title: USA: A bike messenger pioneer puts on the pin stripes.
newsitem.headline: A bike messenger pioneer puts on the pin stripes.

text.p: One small company that claims to have pioneered the bicycle messenger business is now quickly pursuing its second great idea -- running everything from the mail rooms to the copy centres at major corporations.

The company, New-York based Total Management, was founded about 17 years ago and still has one of the biggest fleets of bike messengers in the city, scurrying amid the traffic to rush packages to and from businesses.

Despite the profitability of the bike messenger business, it is a commodity service and competitive. So Total Management decided to branch out and offer a range of services that are tailored to customers outside of their their core business.
Less than 5 percent of major corporations now outsource their operations, but the number is quickly growing and is expected to continue to rise in the future.
A company like Total Management can tailor services to what the customer needs and build a relationship with them. It's called outsourcing in the corporate world.
With this approach, you literally get your foot in the door, so much so that you become a partner with the customer and begin solving their problems rather than just selling them goods.
"It's a deeper relationship and not just based on a transaction," said Valerie Belli, a partner in the company who came aboard to run its marketing operations last year.

Right now Total Management is doing about $25 million a year in business, half of it from the bike messengers. It has offices in New York, Chicago, Columbus and Cincinnati, Ohio, Toronto and Philadelphia and employs about 1,000.
In four years, it projects the business will increase to $100 million, with all the growth coming from its outsourcing services.

The new thrust in the business was enginerred by Michael Fiorito, who bought out an uncle with whom he had built the firm and then won the backing of the Walnut Fund venture capital group in Cincinnati.

With Walnut's advice, the company's internal systems were revamped and a new marketing expert, Belli, brought aboard. She had previously started a services company for a financial printer, Pandick Corp., that was sold after four years in 1989 to Pitney Bowes Inc. for $100 million. She moved to Pitney Bowes with the sale.

But Belli said she grew frustrated at Bowes, as she had at her previous employer, Xerox Corp., because the services that both companies sold were viewed as vehicles to move underlying equipment, like copiers or mail room machinery.
"That gets in the way of a (services) sale," she said, because when you're pushing specific equipment, you can't necessarily offer what the customer needs, if it is made by a competitor.
"When I got the call from Total Management, it was exciting," she said. "The passion was gone and I was both too old and too young not to be doing what I wanted to do."
Along with Belli came Lyle Dampier, who worked his way up from running a copy centre at Harvard University, where he had graduated, to running operations at Pitney Bowes.

With the team in place, Total Management is now offering services to clients like Lehman Bros., where it has more than 90 employees working in shipping and receiving, reception, supplies, and dealing with a 24-hour computer operation. That lets Lehman focus on investment banking -- the business it knows best.
Belli said that initially the cost of the services was about the same as it would cost a company to run its own business, but "after five years, we cost less."
She has also crossed paths with her old employees, who are now competitors, but said that Total Management has an edge: "We buy from anybody and are not related to anyone."
The result is what might be a mantra in the '90s: better service for the customer.
